title: Estate planning: what to leave your children
subtitle: Estate planning basics
openingQuestion: Mr. Binh owns 2 houses, a savings book, and a brokerage account, but dies suddenly without leaving a will. He has a wife and 3 children. Under Vietnamese law, how will his assets be handled?
openingOptions: Only the family's one and only son is eligible to inherit under current law, regardless of the wife or the other daughters
The State will seize all of his assets because he left no will before dying, as if the assets were unclaimed property
Divided under statutory inheritance among the first-priority heirs, which easily leads to disputes
All the assets automatically belong to the eldest child in the family under traditional Vietnamese custom, regardless of current law
explanation: When a person dies without a valid will, assets are divided under 'statutory inheritance' as set out in Vietnam's Civil Code. The first-priority heirs include: spouse, biological and adoptive parents, biological and adopted children of the deceased - people in this group inherit equal shares. A practical problem arises when the asset is real estate that's hard to split evenly (for example, a single house can't be 'cut' into 4 shares for a wife and 3 children), which easily leads to prolonged disputes, sometimes requiring a court to resolve if the parties can't agree themselves.

realWorldExample.company: Real estate inheritance disputes in Vietnam
realWorldExample.description: Courts at every level in Vietnam handle a large volume of civil cases involving inheritance disputes each year, most arising because the deceased left no will, or left a will invalid in form (missing witnesses, not notarized when required). Many cases drag on for years, consuming far more in legal costs than the cost of drafting a will or getting initial legal advice - which might have cost only a few million VND.

quiz.question: If a person dies with no will, on what principle are their assets handled?
options: The eldest son in the family automatically has the sole right to decide how everything is divided
Assets are frozen until a court ruling is issued
Statutory inheritance, divided among the priority heir groups
All assets are transferred into the state budget
quiz.explanation: Vietnam's Civil Code clearly sets out the order of heir groups when there's no will, ensuring assets are divided among the closest relatives under statutory rules.

quiz.question: Why is drafting a valid will considered important, even when the assets aren't very large?
options: Because a will is a mandatory condition for transferring asset ownership
Because a will exempts the heirs from property tax
Because without a will the assets go to the State
Because it accurately reflects intent and reduces the risk of disputes
quiz.explanation: A valid will (in the legally required form, for example notarized or with appropriate witnesses) is the clearest way to express the deceased's wishes, minimizing disputes among heirs.

quiz.question: When a person dies without leaving a will, how are assets divided?
options: Under statutory inheritance, divided equally among the first-priority heir group first
All assets go into the state budget after a three-year waiting period
The eldest child in the family receives the entire estate
Divided according to a verbal agreement the deceased once mentioned to relatives while alive
quiz.explanation: The first-priority heir group includes the spouse, parents, and children - divided equally among them. The outcome can be far from what the deceased actually wanted, and that's the entire reason wills exist.

quiz.question: Which asset is usually NOT divided according to a will?
options: Real estate that was registered solely in the deceased person's name well before the marriage took place
An asset with a named beneficiary already specified, like a life insurance policy
The balance in a savings account at a major commercial bank
Shares in a limited liability company the deceased held equity in
quiz.explanation: A contract with a designated beneficiary pays out directly to the named person, bypassing the inheritance process. This is why beneficiary names should be reviewed after every major family event - an outdated name can override the will entirely.

quiz.question: Why draft a will even when assets aren't yet substantial?
options: Because the law requires everyone over 30 to have drafted a will
Because having a notarized will legally reduces the drafter's annual personal income tax bill
Because it avoids disputes and prolonged procedures that the survivors would have to bear
Because without a will, assets get permanently frozen and can never be divided
quiz.explanation: A will's greatest value isn't dividing wealth - it's reducing the burden: the survivors, already grieving, don't also have to argue and run through months of procedure.

quiz.question: Besides a will, what else should be done so relatives can handle your assets when you die?
options: Withdraw all money from the bank and keep it as cash at home for easy handover
Transfer all assets into the heirs' names right now while still healthy
Keep all financial information secret to prevent relatives from fighting over it early
Make a list of accounts, contracts, and where documents are kept for a trusted person
quiz.explanation: Many families lose money that nobody even knew existed. A simple list - which bank, which insurance contract, where the property documents are - is often more useful than the will itself.

keyTakeaways: With no will, assets are divided under statutory inheritance (first-priority heirs: spouse, parents, children) - not necessarily according to the deceased's actual wishes
Assets that are hard to divide evenly (real estate) are the most common cause of drawn-out inheritance disputes
Drafting a valid will (in the legally required form) clearly expresses intent and reduces the risk of family disputes
An estate plan should be updated periodically, especially after major life events (marriage, divorce, having children, acquiring more assets)

practicePrompt.question: Mrs. Lan has 3 children and a house as her largest asset. She hasn't drafted a will, thinking 'the children will sort it out among themselves.' Why could this be a risky decision, even if the children currently get along well?
options: With no will, the house will be divided under statutory law, which is the most common cause of disputes
There's no risk at all, since the children currently getting along is already enough guarantee they'll always agree later
The only risk is Mrs. Lan having to pay extra inheritance tax if she doesn't draft a will before dying
No need to worry, since the law will automatically divide things exactly according to Mrs. Lan's real wishes even without anything written down
practicePrompt.explanation: Assets that are hard to divide evenly, like real estate, are the most common cause of drawn-out inheritance disputes - drafting a valid will clearly expresses intent and reduces this risk, even if the parties currently get along.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Ask yourself right now
application.message: List the 3 largest assets you currently have (house, savings book, investment account) and ask yourself: if you died suddenly, who would receive them, and would that match what you actually want?
application.secondary: If the answer leaves you unsure, that's a sign to learn more about drafting a will.

sections.text: Nobody wants to think about their own death, so estate planning tends to get put off indefinitely. But it's one of the financial gaps with the heaviest consequences for those left behind - not because of a lack of money, but because of a lack of clarity.

An estate plan simply answers the question: if I died tomorrow, who would my assets (house, land, savings, securities, insurance) transfer to, in what way, and would it cause disputes for those left behind. This isn't a topic reserved for the wealthy - anyone with assets or children should understand the basic principles.
Inheritance by will and statutory inheritance

Vietnamese law recognizes two forms: inheritance by will (if the deceased leaves a valid will, assets are divided exactly as stated in it) and statutory inheritance (if there's no will, or the will is invalid, assets are divided in the order set by the statutory heir groups). The first-priority heir group includes the spouse, biological and adoptive parents, biological and adopted children - these people receive equal shares of the estate if no will states otherwise.

items: A will must be in the legally required form (handwritten with witnesses, or notarized/authenticated) to be valid
The person drafting the will must be of sound mind and acting voluntarily at the time - a will can be ruled invalid by a court if there's a dispute over mental capacity
Even with a will, certain people (minor children, elderly parents unable to work) are still entitled to a minimum statutory share of the estate even if the will doesn't mention them
Marital joint property needs to be clearly identified before dividing an inheritance, to avoid confusing joint property with separate property

sections.label: Why real estate is the most common source of disputes
sections.text: Unlike cash or securities (easy to divide proportionally), a house or plot of land can't be physically split fairly among multiple heirs. The usual options are: sell it and split the proceeds, have one person keep the house and pay the others their share, or hold joint ownership together (which easily creates conflict later when someone wants to sell or use it). This is why many Vietnamese families end up in years-long disputes over an inherited house.
Things worth doing early, not just in old age

Drafting a will doesn't mean expecting something bad to happen - it's like buying insurance: preparing for the worst case to protect the people you love. Simple things you can do early include: clearly listing the assets you currently have (you'll learn to do this in detail in the upcoming personal financial statement lesson), discussing your wishes for dividing assets with your family, and considering a notarized will once your assets are reasonably settled (buying a home, having children).

lines: Estate planning isn't about preparing for death - it's about making sure the people you love don't have to carry extra legal trouble and disputes while grieving.
A clear, valid will today is the most practical gift you can leave behind, no less important than the money you've accumulated.
